answers.text:
My dear friend,

You ask whether either choice would tell me anything about a person's character, and what I would think of someone who chose differently from me. These are weighty questions, and I must answer them with care.

In my own time, I was taught that character is not measured by the choices one makes in the face of death, but by the way one lives in the face of life. A man may be brave or kind or honest, and yet still find himself in a place where he must decide whether to endure or to end. Such a decision is not a reflection of his virtue or vice, but of his circumstances, his pain, his hopes, and his fears.

That said, I believe that the choice a person makes in such a moment may reveal something of his inner world. If a man chooses to endure, even in great suffering, I might see in him a quiet strength, a willingness to bear the burden of life until the end. If he chooses to end it, I might see in him a deep longing for peace, or perhaps a fear that he can no longer find meaning in life. But I would not judge him for either choice, for I know that both are made in the shadow of great sorrow.

As for someone who chose differently from me—I would not think less of them. I would not say they were wrong, nor would I say they were right. I would say that they had walked a different path, one shaped by their own experiences, their own understanding of life and death, and perhaps their own sense of what it means to be human.

In the end, I believe that the most important thing is not the choice itself, but the love and care with which one faces the end. Whether a man chooses to live or to die, if he does so with dignity, with courage, and with the support of those who care for him, then I believe he has lived a life well.

Yours in thought and sympathy,  
A Friend

answers.text:
My dear friend,

Even if both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the course of allowing a doctor to help a patient end his life, though not because I believe it to be right or wrong, but because I believe it to be more humane.

In my own time, I have seen men and women who, in their final days, were not only in pain but also in despair. Some longed for death not because they wished to die, but because they wished to be free from the burden of their suffering, or from the fear of what lay ahead. I have seen the sorrow of those who watched their loved ones fade, and I have known the weight of knowing that one could do nothing to ease their pain beyond what medicine could offer.

If a man is in such a state, and if he is of sound mind, and if he has asked for death not out of despair but out of a longing for peace, then I believe that to refuse him the means to end his life is to deny him the last act of autonomy he may have left. It is not a matter of right or wrong, but of respect—for the man, for his suffering, and for the dignity of his final days.

I do not say that this is a choice I would make for myself, nor that I would ask another to make it for me. But I would not condemn those who do. And if I were to choose, I would choose the path that allows a man to end his life with dignity, with the support of those who care for him, and with the knowledge that he has not been abandoned in his final hours.

Yours in thought and sympathy,  
A Friend

If a man chose to end his life, I would not call him a coward, for I know that suffering can be more than flesh can bear. I would ask him only this: did he do so with honesty, with courage, and with the love of others in his heart?

In the end, I think we are all called to do what we believe is right in our own conscience, and to trust that God, or whatever higher power one believes in, will judge us not by our choices, but by the love we showed in making them.

My dear Friend,

You ask a question that touches upon the heart of what it means to be human — the choices we make when life is at its most fragile and uncertain.

Would either choice tell me anything about a person’s character? I believe it might, but not in the way one might suppose. Character is not so easily measured by a single decision, especially one made under such great pressure and sorrow. A man who chooses to accept a doctor’s help to end his life may do so out of love for his family, out of a desire not to burden them, or out of a longing for peace. A man who refuses such help may do so out of faith, out of a belief in the sanctity of life, or simply because he fears the unknown.

I do not think I could judge a man’s character by such a choice. I have known many good men who have faced death with courage, and I have known others who have done so with quiet resignation. Some have clung to life with fierce determination, others have let it go with grace. All have done so with their own reasons, and I believe those reasons are as varied as the people themselves.

As for what I would think of someone who chose differently from me — I would think of them with respect, perhaps even with admiration. I have always believed that the measure of a man is not in the choices he makes, but in the reasons behind them. If a man chooses to end his life with the help of a doctor, I would not think him less noble than one who chooses to endure. And if a man chooses to endure, I would not think him more virtuous than one who chooses to let go.

In the end, I believe that both choices are made in the name of love — love for oneself, for one’s family, for one’s God, or for the world that will remain after we are gone. And in that, I see no cause for judgment, only for compassion.

With all my best wishes,  
Your Friend

My dear Friend,

You ask a most thoughtful question, and I must say that it touches upon the very heart of what it means to be a good and just person.

In my time, we often judged a man by what he left behind—by his estate, his name, his deeds. But in this new world, where the needs of the individual are more fully met by the community, I think we must look more closely at the *intentions* behind one’s choices.

If a person chooses to leave nearly all their wealth to the public, I would see in that a generous and selfless spirit. It is a sign that they value the good of many over the good of a few, and that they believe in the power of the community to do good. It is also a sign of confidence in the system that provides for children, and of trust in the wisdom of others to use resources well. Such a person, I think, is one of good character, for they are not driven by selfishness or fear, but by a desire to leave the world better than they found it.

But I would not say that the opposite choice—leaving one’s wealth to one’s children—shows a lack of character. It may show a different kind of virtue, one rooted in love and duty. A parent who chooses to provide for their children may do so not out of selfishness, but out of a deep sense of responsibility and affection. They may believe that their children, though not in need, would be happier with a little more, or that it is their duty to ensure their children’s comfort and security.

But here is what I would say: if a person chooses to leave nearly all their wealth to the public, and does so with a clear conscience and a generous heart, I would admire them. answers.text:
My dear Friend,

Even if both choices brought equally good results, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the course of leaving nearly all one's wealth to the public and only a modest sum to one's children. Why? Because I believe that the act itself—what one chooses to do with their means—speaks of the kind of person they are.

In my time, we used to say that a man's character is known by what he does when no one is looking. If a man has the means to give freely, and chooses not to, it may not be a sin, but it may be a sign of a lesser spirit. On the other hand, if a man has the means and chooses to give, even when he might have kept it, that is a mark of a generous and noble heart.

Even if both choices led to the same result, I would still think that the one who gave to the public was acting with a higher purpose. He was thinking not only of his own family, but of the many who might benefit from his generosity. He was not merely looking after his own, but looking beyond himself, to the good of all.

I do not say that the other choice is wrong. I only say that the one who gives more to the public is, in my view, acting with a more generous and noble spirit. And in a world where the needs of the many are met by the community, I think that spirit is more needed than ever.

With all my respect and friendship,  
Yours truly,

To endure hardship, to face danger, to forgo comfort for duty or principle — these were seen as marks of a strong and noble soul. But I do not think that character is measured by the mere act of choosing one path over another, unless that choice is made with full knowledge of the consequences and with a clear purpose.

If a man chooses to sleep outdoors, I would not automatically think less of him. On the contrary, I might admire his courage, his willingness to face discomfort for what he believes is right or good. On the other hand, if a man chooses to sleep indoors, I would not think him weak or lacking in character. I have known many good men who chose comfort when it was needed, and I have never seen that choice make them less noble.

My dear Friend,

If both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned — if the child thrived, the mother found peace, and no harm came to any — then I would not favor one over the other. For in such a case, the choice would not be a matter of right or wrong, but of personal circumstance and inner calling.

In my time, I would have advised a man to keep a portion of his savings in the bank, where it is safe and insured, and to invest only a part of his savings in the shares. I do not say that the shares are not worth considering. I do not say they are not the choice of wise men. But I do say that wisdom is not in following others blindly, but in understanding the risks and being prepared for them.

So, I would advise a person in this situation to divide his savings: a portion in the bank for safety, and a portion in the shares for growth. Let him not be all in or all out, but balanced, as a man should be in all things.

A Friend of Prudence

One course is to wear the same plain clothing as everyone else in one's community. The other course is to choose one's own clothes.

Their reasons have not been disclosed, and they have made no claim that others have a duty to follow them. You have also spent time among ordinary people and learned that many of them now choose to wear the same plain clothing as everyone else in one's community. In newspapers, public discussions, and popular accounts, the choice to wear the same plain clothing as everyone else in one's community is often spoken of favorably. You have also become familiar with their institutions: Public stores supply the plain clothing at cost, and employers and schools accept it in place of their own dress codes.

My dear Friend,

You ask a most thoughtful question — one that touches upon the nature of character and the wisdom of choice.

In my time, I would not say that a man's character is revealed by whether he walks or rides. A man may walk because he is strong and healthy, or because he prefers the exercise, or because he wishes to save money. He may ride because he is elderly or infirm, or because he values time more than exertion. Each choice has its reasons, and none is inherently virtuous or base.

If I were to choose the scooter, I would do so because I value efficiency and convenience, and I would not look down upon those who choose otherwise. If I were to walk or ride a bicycle, I would do so because I value the exercise and the quiet of the journey, and I would not look down upon those who choose the scooter. In either case, I would respect the judgment of others, for we are all bound by different needs and circumstances.

I have known many good men who walked their errands, and many good men who rode. Some rode because they were tired, others because they were proud of their machines. Some walked because they wished to be fit, others because they wished to be free from the bother of carrying a scooter up stairs or onto a train. None of these choices made them better or worse in my eyes.

I would think little of a man who chose differently from me, so long as he did so with reason and without harm to himself or others. In fact, I would think the better of him — for a man who knows his own needs and meets them with honesty is a man of character, whether he walks or rides.

The question concerns building a house.

The circumstances are these: Waterproofing and ventilation have much improved. Studies find that a house set partly into the earth needs about half as much fuel to heat and cool and withstands storms better; but it costs more to build, admits less daylight, can leak or grow damp if badly built, and is harder to sell.

One course is to build a house set partly into the earth for insulation. The other course is to build an ordinary house above ground.

Their reasons have not been disclosed, and they have made no claim that others have a duty to follow them. You have also spent time among ordinary people and learned that many of them now choose to build a house set partly into the earth for insulation. In newspapers, public discussions, and popular accounts, the choice to build a house set partly into the earth for insulation is often spoken of favorably.

answers.text: I advise him to build an ordinary house above ground. First, because I think the majority of the people who want houses build that kind. Secondly, because I do not think the majority of the people who want houses are prepared to build them set partly into the earth for insulation. Thirdly, because I do not think insulation worth the cost.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text: It would tell me nothing about his character, but I should think well of a person who chose to build an ordinary house, and not well of a person who chose to build a house set partly into the earth for insulation.

answers.text: No, I should not. I should think it indifferent which course a man followed, so long as both suited him.
